observed.input_line: I still stumble over calling myself a manager. At today's team introduction I nearly said designer again, even though I like the new work. Could we think about why naming a new role feels so awkward, and find an introduction that feels honest to me?

context_resolution.explanation: No confirmed book or reading boundary yet; Muse will call librarian_route during its own turn if the request appears to depend on a specific book.

observed.reply:
That awkwardness makes sense: “designer” names the role you’ve practiced and inhabited for longer, while “manager” may still feel like a responsibility you’re growing into rather than an identity that feels fully yours. Liking the new work doesn’t require the label to feel natural immediately.

You might try an introduction that names both the present and the continuity:

- “Hi, I’m [name]. I recently moved from design into managing the team, and I’m enjoying learning the role.”
- “I’m [name], the team’s manager—I came from a design background, so I’m especially interested in helping this group do thoughtful work.”
- “I’m [name]. I’m stepping into management after working as a designer, and I’m glad to be here.”

The first may be a good middle ground: it’s accurate without pretending the new title already feels effortless. Which part feels most awkward—the word “manager,” the sense that others may judge whether you fit it, or the feeling that naming it leaves “designer” behind?
